data.summary: Not every trait follows a simple dominant-recessive pattern. In incomplete dominance neither allele is completely dominant, so the heterozygote shows an intermediate phenotype, as when red and white snapdragons produce pink offspring with a 1:2:1 phenotypic ratio. In codominance both alleles are fully and separately expressed in the heterozygote, as with the IA and IB alleles of the ABO blood group system, giving a 1:2:1 ratio in which the heterozygote is a third, distinct phenotype. Where more than two alleles exist for one gene in a population, as with IA, IB and i in the ABO system, the condition is called multiple allelism, although each individual still carries only two alleles.

importantStatements: In incomplete dominance the phenotypic ratio is identical to the genotypic ratio, 1:2:1.
In codominance neither allele masks the other; both are fully expressed in the heterozygote.
Red x white snapdragons give pink flowers because neither allele is completely dominant.
The ABO blood group is controlled by three alleles, IA, IB and i, but each person carries only two of them.
IA and IB are codominant, while i is recessive to both IA and IB.
A type AB person carries both antigens, so can receive from any group but can donate only to AB.

keyPoints: Incomplete dominance: RR x WW gives all RW (pink), and RW x RW gives 1 RR : 2 RW : 1 WW both genotypically and phenotypically.
Codominance: the heterozygote shows both traits fully, as in roan cattle with red and white hair.
Multiple alleles: more than two alleles in a population, but only two in any one individual.
Group A = IAIA or IAi; Group B = IBIB or IBi; Group AB = IAIB; Group O = ii.
Anti-A antibodies occur in group B and O; anti-B antibodies occur in group A and O.
Non-Mendelian crosses still give a 1:2:1 genotypic ratio, but the phenotypes change.
specialNotes: Incomplete dominance is not permanent blending: the alleles remain distinct and can be separated again in a later cross.
Codominance gives two complete traits together, whereas incomplete dominance gives one intermediate trait.
A type AB parent and a type O parent cannot have a type O child, because the AB parent has no i allele to pass on.
Multiple alleles describe the population, not the individual; an individual can never carry three alleles of the same gene.
A type O child proves that each parent contributed an i allele, so neither parent can be type AB or homozygous A or B.
examShortTricks: Incomplete means intermediate, as in pink snapdragons; codominant means both complete, as in AB blood and roan cattle.
A 1:2:1 phenotypic ratio is the signature of both incomplete dominance and codominance, so check what the heterozygote looks like.
For blood group problems, look for the i allele first: a type O child must be ii, so both parents must carry i.
Type AB is a recipient only and type O is a donor only, so the compatibility table is the whole of the question.
examNotes: Matching a phenotype to its type of inheritance, incomplete dominance or codominance, is a frequent one-mark MCQ.
Blood group crosses are the standard numerical, and a type O child from A and B parents is the classic question.
Short answers frequently ask students to differentiate codominance from incomplete dominance with examples.
Always name the example with the concept: snapdragon for incomplete dominance, ABO blood group or roan cattle for codominance.

mcs.explanation: In incomplete dominance the heterozygote has its own intermediate phenotype, so the phenotypic ratio equals the genotypic ratio of 1:2:1.

mcs.explanation: In codominance both alleles are expressed completely and neither masks the other, as in the IAIB blood group.

mcs.question: Which of the following is an example of codominance?
options: Red x white snapdragons giving pink flowers
Rough and smooth texture in peas
mcs.explanation: Blood group AB shows both the A and B antigens fully expressed, which is codominance; pink snapdragons are incomplete dominance.

mcs.question: How many alleles of the ABO blood group gene are present in the human population?
mcs.explanation: The population carries three alleles, IA, IB and i, but any single individual carries only two of them.

mcs.question: A type O individual must have the genotype
mcs.explanation: The i allele is recessive to both IA and IB, so only the homozygous combination ii produces blood group O.
